htb-active.notice: Look for the connection between anonymous SMB access, Group Policy information and service accounts. Notice which exposed detail changes the author’s next question about the Windows domain.
htb-active.reason: Ask why information available through one domain service can affect access elsewhere. Follow the explanation of how credential exposure and service account design create the conditions for Kerberoasting.

htb-bashed.notice: Notice how a development directory becomes relevant to the web shell discovery. Then compare what delegated permissions and writable scripts reveal about the account’s possible next actions.
htb-bashed.reason: Ask why a script’s ownership, write permissions and execution context must be considered together. The useful lesson is how those relationships can change the privileges available to an account.

htb-blue.notice: Focus on the SMB service identified during enumeration and the evidence about its patch status. Notice why the author treats that finding as the main decision point.
htb-blue.reason: Ask why an unpatched network service can expose administrative capabilities before a separate local escalation is needed. Connect the EternalBlue discussion to the importance of patch management.

htb-devel.notice: Watch how anonymous FTP access relates to the web directory rather than treating them as separate findings. Notice the significance of executable uploads and missing Windows patches.
htb-devel.reason: Ask why file placement becomes more serious when a web service can execute those files. Then consider how missing patches affect the privileges available after initial access.

htb-jerry.notice: Identify how the author connects Tomcat management, weak credentials and application deployment. Notice which management capability matters after authentication, rather than focusing only on the password discovery.
htb-jerry.reason: Ask why access to an application manager can carry more power than access to an ordinary web page. Relate the deployment feature to the reverse shell discussion.

htb-lame.notice: Compare the evidence behind the unsuccessful FTP route with the later Samba investigation. Notice how service enumeration helps the author change direction when an early idea fails.
htb-lame.reason: Ask why discovering a service is only the start of evaluating a possible route. The comparison helps explain why observed behaviour should guide the next hypothesis.

htb-legacy.notice: Follow the relationship between SMB discovery, vulnerability validation and the manual approach. Pay attention to the compatibility questions the author encounters when working with an older Windows system.
htb-legacy.reason: Ask why identifying a vulnerability does not automatically make every available tool suitable. Relate the legacy tooling discussion to the need to match an approach to the environment.

htb-mirai.notice: Notice how the Pi-hole page influences the author’s thinking about the underlying device. Then distinguish the credential investigation from the later search involving mounted USB storage.
htb-mirai.reason: Ask why a visible application can suggest a useful device hypothesis without proving it. Consider how default credentials and storage layout affect different parts of the investigation.

htb-nibbles.notice: Track the clues that connect the sparse web page to Nibbleblog. Notice how exposed information, an upload feature and script permissions each influence a different decision.
htb-nibbles.reason: Ask why an upload capability must be considered alongside the application’s behaviour, and why a script’s permissions matter later. Focus on how separate weaknesses can support one another.

htb-optimum.notice: Look for the service version evidence that leads the author toward HTTP File Server. Compare the initial access approaches before following the discussion of local Windows exploit selection.
htb-optimum.reason: Ask why service version information is useful evidence but still needs interpretation. Consider why the conditions for initial access and later privilege escalation require separate evaluation.

htb-shocker.notice: Notice why checking file extensions changes the web discovery process. Follow the connection from the CGI script to Shellshock, then examine what the sudo rule permits.
htb-shocker.reason: Ask why finding the right endpoint can matter as much as choosing a vulnerability. Relate the final permissions discussion to the privileges granted by a sudo rule.

htb-valentine.notice: Pause at the author’s hints and separate what is known from what is assumed. Track how Heartbleed, the encrypted SSH key and the tmux session become connected.
htb-valentine.reason: Ask why information exposure, key protection and shared sessions belong to different security boundaries. Consider how a weakness in one boundary can make another clue more useful.

thm-rootme.notice: Look for the evidence connecting hidden directories to the upload feature. After the limited web account appears, notice which Linux permission details change the direction of the investigation.
thm-rootme.reason: Ask why uploading a file and obtaining elevated access are different security questions. Connect the account’s limited privileges to the later discussion of SUID and permission boundaries.

thm-pickle-rick.notice: Follow the small website clues that lead to credentials and the command panel. Notice the difference between the panel’s command restrictions and the account’s sudo permissions.
thm-pickle-rick.reason: Ask why filtering selected command names offers a different kind of control from limiting account privileges. Consider how these two controls affect what the panel can accomplish.

thm-blue.notice: Start with the Windows service scan and the evidence used to select a vulnerability. Then distinguish the Metasploit session discussion from the later administrative access and password hash findings.
thm-blue.reason: Ask why service vulnerabilities, session capabilities and account privileges are related but separate ideas. Follow how the author uses expected results to explain each change in access.

thm-basic-pentesting.notice: Follow how service discovery supports user identification before the password investigation begins. Notice when the exposed SSH key changes the question from initial access to another account.
thm-basic-pentesting.reason: Ask why knowing a username, knowing a password and possessing an SSH key represent different pieces of evidence. Consider how their combination can affect an account boundary.

thm-vulnversity.notice: Pay attention to the web service beyond the default ports and the upload form’s restrictions. Later, notice what makes the service manager’s SUID permissions worth investigating.
thm-vulnversity.reason: Ask why file restrictions and operating system permissions need separate analysis. The reading connects web application behaviour with the privileges under which a local program can run.

thm-linux-fundamentals-part-1.notice: Notice how each terminal concept answers a practical question: who you are, where files are, what they contain and how to save output. Expect revised task numbering.
thm-linux-fundamentals-part-1.reason: Ask why navigation, searching and output handling appear throughout later walkthroughs. These skills help turn raw terminal results into evidence you can locate, compare and understand.
